questions.topic: What the scope of a mobilisation required
questions.learningObjective: Identify the population a mobilisation plan reaches.
questions.stem: A mobilisation table lists every trade in the county, from shipwright to schoolmaster, beside the number of men each trade can release.

options.text: It shows the call reaching into civilian trades, not only men already in uniform
It shows that only men who enlisted voluntarily in the first months were counted
options.misconception: Believes mobilisation relies on volunteers, not the register

options.text: It shows the number of rifles each trade could supply rather than the men in it
options.misconception: Confuses the register of men with a table of equipment

options.text: It shows that the army planned to call men by county quota and close the list
options.misconception: Confuses a quota allocation with the scope of registration

questions.explanation: The trade list shows the plan reaching into civilian work, so a register was needed rather than a call on volunteers. Reading it as a quota or an equipment list misses who is covered.
questions.hint: Ask what the rows represent, not what they are counted for.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the scope of a mobilisation required
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a two-column capacity table implies about the scope of a mobilisation.
questions.stem: A second table beside the mobilisation list separates essential at home from available to the colours and gives each class a headcount.

answer.exemplar: The table does not treat the army's needs as the only measure of the state's capacity. It counts what must stay at home as carefully as what can be sent, so the scope of mobilisation is a balance of two columns rather than a single demand. What it leaves to the registrar is how one employer's claim of indispensability is weighed against another when two towns swear the same trade is essential.

questions.explanation: The two columns measure capacity from both ends, so mobilisation scope is a balance, not a single demand. The table leaves the registrar to weigh one employer's claim against another's.
questions.hint: The table counts what stays as well as what goes.

The table records the men who enlisted before the list of the twenty-one to thirty was drawn

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a draw by lot produced an order of call.
questions.stem: A district board table records a serially numbered slip for each registered man and a separate column for the number drawn in each lot.

answer.exemplar: Giving each registered man a number and then drawing those numbers at random removed favour from the order of call, so the sequence of summonses followed chance rather than a neighbour's connections. What the method left open was everything before and after the draw: the board still decided which men were numbered at all, which trades counted as essential, how long a deferment might last, and whether a man who slipped a number could be found and called again.

questions.explanation: Numbering men and then drawing the numbers made the sequence of summons a matter of chance rather than favour. The method did not touch who was numbered, exempted or lost from the list.
questions.hint: Separate the draw's fairness from the list's fairness.

options.text: Slip 12, listed in the second year's calls because the early numbers were spent
options.misconception: Assumes a second year began only after every early number

questions.hint: Consider which number and which session the slip records.

questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Infer how the order of call was made from a board minute.

stimulus.body: The drawing was held at the county court house with the press present, as the law requires. Order came from the board's own judgement of each man's trade and circumstances

options.misconception: Ignores the drawing and reads in a pre-sorted list

options.text: Order came from the date on which each man had first registered in the district
options.misconception: Assumes registration order was the order of call

questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Identify the method of drawing from a contemporary newspaper account.

stimulus.body: Crowds filled the hall at the county court house to watch the drum turned, and by evening the first nine thousand names of the district were posted on the door. questions.stem: The account accompanies the table of drawn numbers. What does it show about the method of drawing?

options.text: Chance governed the sequence, and a number could not be transferred to another man
Priority went to those who had served first, so veterans were drawn ahead of others
options.misconception: Reads one veteran's early number as a standing rule

options.text: Men chose their own number by paying a fee, which is why the crowd was so large
options.misconception: Finds a fee scheme in an account that forbids it

options.text: The board settled the sequence in secret, and the public drawing was a formality
options.misconception: Treats a public, witnessed draw as a secret allocation

questions.explanation: A veteran and county men of no service appear in the same first batch, and the notice forbids trading numbers, the signature of a random draw. The other options find priorities, fees or secrecy.
questions.hint: Note who is in the first batch and what the notice forbids.

options.misconception: Believes the draw alone makes the whole scheme impartial

options.text: A random draw that sorted men fairly, leaving the exemptions unexamined

options.misconception: Denies a documented public draw in favour of a hidden list

stimulus.body: Bonds of ten dollars, one hundred dollars and one thousand dollars are on sale at post offices, banks and schoolhouses until the end of the month. questions.learningObjective: Determine what a campaign poster adds to the ledger of subscriptions.

stimulus.body: Buy a bond and take it home to your own family. The note is yours to keep, and the interest is yours to spend. questions.topic: Features of a war bond campaign
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of estimates with actual subscriptions shows.
questions.stem: A treasurer's table compares what each bond issue raised with the estimate made when the drive was announced.

answer.exemplar: Each estimate was met or exceeded, which tells the treasurer that the appeal had been widely taken up and that the state could plan on the money. What the table cannot show is who bore the cost. A subscription may be money saved from wages, a loan taken against a shop, or a payment by a family that had already given a son, and the columns look identical in all three cases.

questions.explanation: The comparison shows the appeal was widely answered and the state could rely on the proceeds. It cannot show who paid, because savings, a loan and a second gift appear in the same column.

questions.topic: Naming the domestic opponent an accomplice
questions.learningObjective: Infer the definition of the domestic opponent from a proclamation.

stimulus.body: Any man who obstructs the recruiting service, or incites others to do so, shall be subject to the penalties provided by law. All loyal citizens are urged to report to the proper authorities any persons who are so acting, and to give such aid as may lead to their conviction. Firms that release workers to such activity will be reported.

options.text: The opponent was a soldier refusing overseas service, ending voluntary enlistment
options.misconception: Confuses the enemy at home with a soldier declining to serve

questions.explanation: The proclamation makes obstruction of recruiting the offence and asks citizens to report it, so the domestic opponent became whoever obstructed. The others narrow the category to foreigners or trade.

questions.topic: Naming the domestic opponent an accomplice

questions.explanation: The table sets registration before the call because a call can only be made from a list of names, and the expected number follows from that register. The others collapse or invert the steps.
questions.hint: Which column has to exist before the others matter?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a draw by lot was used and what the comparison leaves unresolved.
questions.stem: A board table compares the number of men summoned in a district with the number who had volunteered before the law required a register.

answer.exemplar: The comparison shows that a summons list far larger than the volunteer list could not have been made from anyone's judgement of who deserved to go, because too many men were to be called and no one's opinion of them could be recorded quickly enough. It does not settle whether the register itself was fair, since the table counts only the volunteers and the summoned men, and says nothing about who was left out of the numbered slips at all.

questions.explanation: A summons list too large to sort by hand or favour had to be ordered mechanically, which the comparison between volunteers and summoned men shows. It says nothing about who was numbered.
questions.hint: Compare the two numbers, then ask what they leave out.

Law against obstruction passed, war declared, trials begin, amendment on sedition passed

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The intent clause and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: Explain the choice behind an intent clause from a drafting commentary.

stimulus.body: Two clauses were offered to the committee. The first asked whether the act was done with the intent to obstruct, and the second asked whether the act was done with the intent to assist the enemy. The committee rejected the second as too near to a matter of opinion, and preferred a test that a court could put to a jury in words that men could understand.

questions.stem: The commentary is filed with the table of drafting choices. What does it show about the intent clause?

options.text: The government chose a clause a jury could apply, over one it thought too vague
The government wanted no mental element at all, and the clause was a last-minute addition
options.misconception: Reverses the committee's choice of an intent requirement

options.text: The committee was divided over whether the offence should exist, and settled it on wording
options.misconception: Reads a drafting preference as a dispute over the offence

options.text: The clause was drafted to make conviction easier, and the committee said so in its report
options.misconception: Attributes a stated purpose the commentary does not mention

questions.explanation: The committee rejected the clause aimed at assisting the enemy as too much a matter of opinion and kept the one a jury could apply. This was a drafting choice, not a dispute about the offence.
questions.hint: The rejected clause is the clue to why one was preferred.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What actually limited wartime shipbuilding
questions.learningObjective: Read an official return for the real limit on building.

stimulus.body: Ships completed during the year: 120, of which 88 were wooden hulls and 32 were steel. Steel hulls under construction at the year's end: 9, an increase of four on the year before, but the builders report that the increase was achieved by working the existing slips later into the night rather than by laying down any new slipway. Deliveries of plate fell short of the orders in eleven of the twelve months.

questions.stem: The return is printed above the table of output. What does the return show about what limited building?

options.text: Growth came from longer hours in existing yards while plate deliveries lagged behind orders
Growth came from new slipways, since the number of hulls under construction rose
options.misconception: Ignores the return's statement about working existing slips

options.text: Growth came from steel construction replacing wood, since steel hulls outnumbered wooden
options.misconception: Reverses the proportions of steel and wooden hulls

options.text: Growth came from a rise in plate deliveries, since the orders were met in eleven months
options.misconception: Turns a shortfall in deliveries into a rise in deliveries

questions.explanation: The return attributes the increase in hulls to longer hours on existing slips and records plate deliveries short of orders in nearly every month, so inputs and slips set the limit.
questions.hint: Check the hull counts and the months of short deliveries.

The rule failed because the officials who set it did not know the wholesale price in the county
options.misconception: Blames the setter's knowledge, not the effect of a ceiling

options.misconception: Finds the cause in dealer numbers, not in the price

options.text: The rule worked until the shopkeepers began charging the official price without any shortage
options.misconception: Claims the shortage vanished once prices were posted

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the scope of a mobilisation required
questions.learningObjective: Explain who decided the scope of a mobilisation from a district table.
questions.stem: A table of districts lists for each the number registered, the number claimed exempt on occupational grounds, and the number of claims the board allowed.

answer.exemplar: The table makes the board visible as a filter between a law that registered every eligible man and the narrower number who were actually called. The number of claims allowed shows how much discretion was used, and the number not allowed shows the pressure under which it was exercised. What the table leaves out is the reasoning: it counts allowed and refused claims without recording why any of them was decided either way.

questions.explanation: The allowed and refused claim counts make the district board the filter between registration and call, and show discretion used under pressure. The table counts decisions without reasons.
questions.hint: Compare the claims made with the claims allowed.

questions.topic: Drawing the order of call by lot
questions.learningObjective: Select the description that matches the method of fixing the order of call.
questions.stem: Four descriptions of the order of call are offered. Which one correctly describes the method used to fix the sequence of summons?

options.text: Each registered man was given a number, and the numbers were drawn in public to set the order
Men were summoned in the order of their registration, so the earliest applicant went first
options.misconception: Describes a seniority rule rather than a draw

options.text: Each district was given a quota and the order inside it was settled by the board's vote
options.misconception: Describes a quota system as though it fixed the sequence

options.text: Men were placed in classes by trade and called class by class from the most needed trade down
options.misconception: Confuses the classification of trades with the order of call

questions.explanation: Numbering each registered man and drawing the numbers at random is what fixed the sequence, so the summons order was not registration date, board vote or trade priority.
questions.hint: Look for the step that establishes chance, not priority.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Naming the domestic opponent an accomplice
questions.learningObjective: Conclude what a summary of the wartime statutes shows about the domestic opponent.

stimulus.kind: closing summary of the wartime acts
stimulus.body: The measures of 1917 and 1918 did two things at once. They gave the government the men and the money it needed, and they gave prosecutors a way to describe ordinary men who disliked the war as allies of the enemy power. The second use was never the stated purpose of the statutes, and the committee that reported on them said so in terms, noting that a man might be prosecuted for what he said without any proof that he had meant any harm to the country.

questions.stem: The summary is printed above the table of the wartime statutes. What does the summary show about the domestic opponent?

options.text: A category created for wartime need, then used to reach opinion rather than conspiracy
A category created after the war by critics who wished to explain the prosecutions
options.misconception: Dates the category after the period in which it operated

options.text: A category so narrow in law that it could never have reached a man for his opinions
options.misconception: Claims a narrow test that the prosecutions contradict

options.text: A category created to protect dissent, with the statutes written to limit prosecutions
options.misconception: Reverses the purpose the statutes were serving

questions.explanation: The statutes were made to serve wartime need, and the summary says they were then used to reach opinion without proof of harmful intent. The alternatives misdate the category or reverse its purpose.
questions.hint: Note the phrase about no proof of harm to the country.
